data.text:
For a long time, I had ideas.
Some were small. Some were ridiculous. Some were probably never going to become anything. And, as usually happens with ideas, most of them stayed exactly where they started — in my head.
I think the difference now is that I finally started doing something about them.
Not because I suddenly became an expert at programming. Quite the opposite.
A lot of the things I've built recently started with me not knowing how to build them.
I'd learn something because I needed it. I'd break something. Fix it. Break something else. Ask questions. Read documentation. Try again. Sometimes I'd spend an unreasonable amount of time figuring out why something that should have worked simply didn't.
And somewhere along the way, building stopped feeling like something I should learn and started feeling like something I genuinely enjoy doing.
It started with small things
I didn't begin with some grand plan to build a collection of applications.
I just wanted to make things.
Prime started as an idea for managing my own finances. Not another complicated financial platform, but something that could answer a simple question: Where do I actually stand financially?
Then came Curio — an attempt to build a place for the things I find interesting and don't want to lose. Not another productivity system demanding that I read, organise, tag and optimise everything. Just a quiet little library for curiosity.
Vault came from a different place: wanting something personal, local and under my control instead of handing something as important as passwords to another service without thinking about it.
Wayfarer is a different kind of experiment altogether — and probably the least practical of the lot. It's a game idea inspired by the kind of place I actually live in: a small Himalayan town, ordinary people, familiar roads, schools, shops, streams and mountains.
I don't know exactly where it will go.
That's part of the fun.
I also learned that building isn't the same as knowing
One of the most useful things I've discovered is that I don't need to know everything before starting.
I used Flutter without really knowing Flutter.
I learned Git because I needed version control.
I learned about deployment because I wanted my website to actually exist on the internet.
I learned about Cloudflare because apparently getting a website from "it works on my computer" to "it works for everyone" involves a surprising number of things.
There were plenty of moments where something broke and I had absolutely no idea why.
But that stopped being a reason not to build.
It became part of building.
The process became something like:
Have an idea → figure out what I don't know → learn enough to continue → build → break it → fix it → learn something else.
And repeat.
The website became part of the experiment
Eventually I realised that I didn't just want a GitHub profile full of repositories.
I wanted a place that felt like mine. Something quiet, something curious — somewhere that could hold the things I'm making, the things I'm learning, and eventually the things I'm thinking about.
That's what this website is supposed to be.
Not a résumé dressed up as a website.
Not a collection of buzzwords.
Not a place where everything has to look polished and successful.
Just a record of the things I'm curious enough to make.
I'm still figuring it out
I don't consider myself a finished developer. Honestly, I'm not sure I even want to be "finished."
I want to make better apps. I want to make games. I want to understand more about how computers actually work. I want to experiment with local AI. I want to make weird little tools that solve problems nobody else cares about.
Some ideas will work. Some will be abandoned. Some will probably be terrible.
That's okay. The important thing is that they won't all remain ideas.
That's probably the biggest change.
I started building things again.
And now I don't really want to stop.
